title: Checkpoint: Working with Data
intro: Check that you can load and filter tables with pandas, summarize them, and draw clear charts with matplotlib.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Tashkent", "Bukhara", "Samarkand"],
                   "temp": [31.5, 28.1, 33.0]})
print(df.iloc[1]["city"], df.loc[2, "temp"])
questions.explanation: .iloc selects by position (row 1 is Bukhara), and .loc selects by label (index 2 is Samarkand's row).

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?
questions.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Tashkent", "Bukhara"], "temp": [31.5, 28.1]})
print(df["city", "temp"])
options: It prints only the city column
questions.explanation: Single brackets look for one column named by the tuple ("city", "temp"). Pass a list: df[["city", "temp"]].

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({"product": ["Tea", "Halva"], "qty": [2, 1]})
prices = pd.DataFrame({"product": ["Tea"], "price": [15000]})
print(len(orders.merge(prices, on="product")), len(orders.merge(prices, on="product", how="left")))
questions.explanation: An inner merge keeps only products found in both tables (Tea). A left merge keeps every order and fills the missing price with NaN.

questions.question: What happens when this code runs?
questions.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"temp": [31.5, 28.1], "humidity": [22, 30]})
print(df[df["temp"] > 30 and df["humidity"] < 25])
questions.explanation: and needs a single True or False, but each comparison gives a whole Series. Use & with parentheses around each condition.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
import pandas as pd
sales = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Tashkent", "Bukhara", "Tashkent"],
                      "quantity": [4, 12, 6]})
print(sales.groupby("city")["quantity"].sum()["Tashkent"])
questions.explanation: groupby collects the rows for each city, and sum() adds Tashkent's quantities: 4 + 6.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
import pandas as pd
sales = pd.DataFrame({"product": ["tea", "plov", "tea", "tea"]})
counts = sales["product"].value_counts()
print(counts.index[0], counts.iloc[0])
questions.explanation: value_counts() counts each value and sorts from most to least common, so tea with 3 comes first.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"name": [" aziza", "BEKZOD "]})
print(df["name"].str.strip().str.title().tolist())
questions.explanation: The .str accessor applies string methods to every value in the column, and they can be chained.

questions.question: What does the print show?
questions.code:
import pandas as pd
sales = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Tashkent", "Bukhara"], "price": [15000, 8000]})
sales[sales["city"] == "Bukhara"]["price"] = 9000
print(sales.loc[1, "price"])
questions.explanation: Chained indexing assigns into a temporary copy, so the original is unchanged. Use sales.loc[sales["city"] == "Bukhara", "price"] = 9000.

questions.question: What happens on the last line?
questions.code:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.title("Sales")
options: The title is set to Sales
questions.explanation: ax.title is a Text object, not a method. On an Axes use ax.set_title("Sales").

questions.question: You want to see how daily temperatures are distributed across a year. Which chart fits best?
options: A line chart of the months' names
A scatter plot with one point
questions.explanation: A histogram groups values into bins and shows how often each range occurs, which is exactly a distribution.
